why_how.text: Drivers under eighteen have a much higher crash rate, so North Carolina treats every one of them as a provisional licensee.
Driver education comes first, so a teen arrives at the permit test with classroom learning and real time behind the wheel.

scenario.text: Avery is fifteen, lives in North Carolina, and wants to start learning in the family car.

reasoning.text: Avery fits the Level One age range, so Avery first finishes driver education with thirty classroom hours and six behind the wheel, then brings the certificate.

result.text: With a parent signing, Avery takes the written, sign and vision tests for the Level One permit.

claim.text: Common mistake: mixing up the driver education hours as six in the classroom and thirty behind the wheel.

correction.text: The certificate shows at least thirty classroom hours and at least six hours behind the wheel.

prompt.text: Avery, age fifteen, wants to test for the Level One permit next week. What must Avery bring before testing?

answer.text: The driver education certificate showing at least thirty classroom hours and six behind-the-wheel hours.

rationale.text: Drivers under eighteen show the driver education certificate before testing for a permit or a license.

lines.text: Every driver under eighteen is provisional.
Level One is the first step.

narration.text: This chapter is about graduated licensing, the step-by-step path North Carolina uses for its youngest drivers. Every driver under eighteen is a provisional licensee, and special laws apply because this group has a much higher crash rate than older drivers. The path has three levels, and each one loosens the rules a little as experience grows. In this first lesson you will learn who the Level One Limited Learner Permit is for, the driver education certificate you need before any test, which tests you pass, and whose signature the application needs.

The Level One Limited Learner Permit is for North Carolina residents who are at least fifteen but under eighteen and who will drive vehicles needing a Class C license, the ordinary car license. Because the applicant is a minor, a parent or legal guardian must sign for the permit. Keep the age window in mind, because the next level starts at sixteen. If a practice question describes a fifteen-year-old who wants to begin learning, Level One is the answer. If it describes someone eighteen or older, the regular learner permit from the testing chapter applies instead.

Before taking the permit test, a teen must show a certificate for an approved driver education course. That course includes at least thirty hours in the classroom and six hours behind the wheel. The rule is broader than the permit alone. Any driver under eighteen must show this certificate before testing for either a learner permit or a license. Once the certificate is in hand, the Level One applicant must pass the written, sign and vision tests. So the order is clear: finish driver education, bring the certificate, then sit the three tests with a parent or guardian signing.

Here is a small trap with a big payoff. The driver education certificate carries two numbers, and practice questions like to swap them. The classroom part is at least thirty hours. The behind-the-wheel part is at least six hours. A distractor that offers six classroom hours and thirty behind the wheel looks almost right, but it reverses the two. One way to keep them straight is that the classroom is where you spend most of the time, learning rules and judgment, while the shorter behind-the-wheel portion starts building skill that the permit stage will grow much further.

Here is a quick check: Avery is fifteen, lives in North Carolina, and wants to test for the Level One permit next week. What must Avery bring before testing? Work it out before reading on. The answer is the driver education certificate, showing at least thirty classroom hours and six hours behind the wheel. Every driver under eighteen shows that certificate before testing for a permit or a license. Then Avery passes the written, sign and vision tests, and because Avery is a minor, a parent or legal guardian signs for the permit.

Let us pull it together. Every driver under eighteen is a provisional licensee, because young drivers have a much higher crash rate. The Level One permit is for North Carolina residents at least fifteen but under eighteen who will drive Class C vehicles. Before testing for any permit or license, a driver under eighteen shows a driver education certificate with at least thirty classroom hours and six behind-the-wheel hours. The Level One applicant passes the written, sign and vision tests, and a parent or legal guardian signs. Next, we look at the rules for driving at Level One.

title.text: Level One rules on the road

why_how.text: Level One always pairs the teen with an experienced supervising driver, because the permit stage is for learning under guidance.
The first six months add an hour limit, because new drivers face the most risk while skills are brand new.
Phones are banned because distraction is dangerous for every new driver; only true emergency calls are allowed.

scenario.text: Kai has had a Level One permit for seven months and wants to drive to a late movie at ten at night with a grandparent beside Kai.

reasoning.text: After six months, Level One allows driving at any hour, but always with a supervising driver such as a grandparent licensed at least five years.

result.text: Kai may make the trip, with every passenger belted and only Kai and the grandparent in front.

claim.text: Many people think a Level One holder may drive alone once the first six months are over.

correction.text: After six months the hours open up, but a supervising driver is still required in both Level One phases.

prompt.text: Kai's Level One permit is four months old. Can Kai drive with a parent at ten at night?

answer.text: No. In the first six months Level One driving is limited to five in the morning until nine at night.

rationale.text: The any-hour phase starts only after six months, and even then a supervising driver is required.

title.text: Driving on a Level One permit

narration.text: Now that you have the permit, what can you actually do with it? This lesson covers the rules for driving at Level One. You will learn who can be your supervising driver, the two time phases that control when you may drive, the seat belt and front-seat rules, and the cell phone ban with its short list of emergency exceptions. These rules work together. A Level One driver is always learning beside an experienced adult, with fewer distractions and safer hours, so that the skills built here carry forward when the rules start to loosen at Level Two.

lines.text: Or an adult the parent approves.
Licensed for at least five years.

narration.text: A supervising driver must be a parent, a grandparent or a guardian, or a responsible adult that the parent or guardian approves. That person must hold a valid license, and the license must have been held for at least five years. So an older sibling who got a license last year does not qualify, even if they are careful and willing. The five-year rule is about experience. The supervisor is there to coach, spot hazards and step in, and the state wants that person to have years of driving behind them, not a few months.

lines.text: First six months: five to nine.

narration.text: Level One has two time phases. For the first six months, a Level One permit holder may drive only from five in the morning until nine at night, and only with the supervising driver. Once six months have passed since the permit was issued, the holder may drive at any hour of the day or night. But notice what does not change. The supervising driver is still required. The second phase widens the clock, not the freedom to drive alone. That pattern of loosening one rule while keeping another is common across graduated licensing, so watch for it.

Here is the trap. Because the hour limit disappears after six months, many learners assume the supervisor requirement disappears too. It does not. Level One has two time phases, limited hours first and any hour after that, but a supervising driver is required in both phases. On practice questions, an option that lets a Level One driver go alone, even late in the permit period, is wrong. Driving alone begins at Level Two. So for Level One, keep this line ready: the hours open, but the supervisor stays in the passenger seat beside you.

lines.text: Every passenger belted or in a child seat.
Only driver and supervisor in front.

narration.text: Inside the car, Level One has two seating rules. Every passenger must wear a seat belt or ride in a child safety seat. And only the driver and the supervising driver may sit in front. Friends or siblings ride in the back, belted. This front-seat rule belongs to Level One specifically. Level Two handles passengers differently, with limits on how many young passengers may ride, as you will see later. So when a question asks which stage reserves the front seat for the driver and the supervisor alone, the answer is Level One.

lines.text: No cell phone or connected phone tech.

narration.text: A Level One driver may not use a cell phone or any connected cell-phone technology while driving on a public street, highway or public vehicular area. That includes hands-free connections, not only holding the phone. The only exception for a teen driver is an emergency call to an emergency operator, a hospital, a doctor's office or clinic, an ambulance service, a fire department, a law enforcement agency, or a parent, legal guardian or spouse. A call to a friend for directions, or to order food, is not on the list. Emergencies only.

lines.text: Driving with a parent at ten at night?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Kai's Level One permit was issued four months ago. Tonight Kai wants to drive to a friend's house at ten at night, with a parent in the front passenger seat. Is that allowed? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. In the first six months, Level One driving is limited to five in the morning until nine at night, and ten at night falls outside that window. After six months the clock opens to any hour, but even then a supervising driver must be beside Kai on every trip. Patience now pays off later.

lines.text: Five to nine for six months.
Front seat for two, no phone.

narration.text: To wrap up, a Level One supervising driver is a parent, grandparent, guardian or approved adult who has held a valid license for at least five years. For the first six months, a Level One holder may drive only from five in the morning until nine at night, always supervised. After six months, any hour is allowed, still supervised. Every passenger is belted or in a child seat, and only the driver and supervisor sit in front. Phones and connected phone technology are banned, except emergency calls to the listed people and services.

why_how.text: Level Two needs both time and practice, so the state counts months held and hours logged as two separate requirements.
A clean recent record shows the teen is ready for more freedom before it is granted.

scenario.text: Sam has held a Level One permit for nine months and logged sixty-five hours, including eight at night.

reasoning.text: Sam meets the nine-month hold, but the log needs at least ten night hours, and Sam has only eight.

result.text: Sam keeps driving with a supervisor after sunset until the log shows at least ten night hours.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a long driving log can make up for a shorter time holding the permit.

correction.text: The nine-month hold and the sixty-hour log with ten at night are different requirements, and both apply before Level Two.

prompt.text: Sam has held Level One for nine months with sixty-five logged hours, eight of them at night. Is Sam ready to apply?

answer.text: Not yet. The log needs at least ten night hours.

rationale.text: The holding period is met, but the log requirement is separate and needs ten hours after sunset.

narration.text: This lesson covers what it takes to leave Level One behind. Moving up to the Level Two Limited Provisional License is not automatic. A teen has to hold the permit long enough, practice enough hours with a supervisor, document that practice in a driving log, and keep a clean record in the months just before applying. You will learn how long the permit must be held, how many hours the log needs, how day and night driving are defined, who signs the log and when it is turned in, and which convictions block the move up.

lines.text: Hold Level One for nine months.
At least ten of them at night.

narration.text: Two requirements sit at the heart of Level One. First, a teen must keep the Level One permit for nine months before applying for the Limited Provisional License. Second, the Level One driving log must record at least sixty hours behind the wheel, and at least ten of those hours must be at night. Both are minimums, so more practice is always welcome. The nine months give time for many kinds of weather, traffic and road types to show up, and the logged hours make sure that time is actually spent driving. Both clocks must run out.

lines.text: After sunset with no daylight is night.

narration.text: For the log, daytime driving means the time from sunrise to sunset while there is daylight, and night driving means after sunset when there is no daylight. Night is defined by the sky, not by a clock time. The supervising driver signs the driving log, and it is turned in to the Division when the teen applies for the Limited Provisional License. One more gate stands in the way. To move up to Level Two, the teen must have had no moving violation, seat belt or cell phone convictions during the previous six months. Every rule here has a purpose.

lines.text: Sixty hours, ten at night, is the log.

narration.text: Here is where learners slip. The Level One holding period is nine months, while the driving log needs at least sixty hours with ten at night. These are different requirements, and both apply before Level Two. A huge log does not shorten the nine months, and nine months of holding the permit does not excuse a thin log. Practice questions mix the numbers, for example sixty months or nine hours, or they claim one requirement can replace the other. Keep them in separate boxes. The calendar counts months; the log counts hours.

Here is a quick check: Sam has held a Level One permit for nine months and has logged sixty-five hours behind the wheel, eight of them after sunset with no daylight. Sam has a clean record. Is Sam ready to apply for Level Two? Work it out before reading on. Not yet. The nine-month hold is met, and the total hours pass sixty, but the log needs at least ten hours at night, and Sam has only eight. A few more supervised drives after dark will finish the requirement, and then the supervisor signs the log for the application.

Let us recap the move up. A teen keeps the Level One permit for nine months. The signed driving log shows at least sixty hours behind the wheel, with at least ten at night, where night means after sunset with no daylight. The supervising driver signs the log, and it goes to the Division with the Limited Provisional License application. And the teen must have no moving violation, seat belt or cell phone convictions in the previous six months. When all of that is in place, Level Two is next, with its first taste of driving alone.

why_how.text: Level Two lets a teen drive alone for the first time, but only in safer hours and with tight limits on young passengers.
Young passengers raise crash risk for teen drivers, so the limit counts under-twenty-one riders from outside the household.

scenario.text: Lee, age sixteen with a Level Two license, drives alone with a friend from another family and a younger brother.

reasoning.text: Under-twenty-one household members may not ride along while an under-twenty-one passenger from outside the household is aboard.

result.text: Lee may carry the friend or the brother on this unsupervised trip, but not both together.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a Level Two driver may never carry any passenger under twenty-one when driving alone.

correction.text: One under-twenty-one passenger from outside the household is allowed, plus one more only for a direct school trip, and household-only groups have no limit.

prompt.text: Lee drives alone at Level Two with one friend from another family. A second friend also needs a ride to the mall. Can Lee take both?

answer.text: No. Only one under-twenty-one passenger from outside the household is allowed, unless the extra rider is a student going directly to or from school.

rationale.text: The extra passenger exception is only for a student on a direct school trip, and a mall trip does not qualify.

narration.text: Level Two is a milestone, because it is the first time a teen may drive without a supervisor. The Level Two Limited Provisional License is for drivers at least sixteen but under eighteen, and the word limited matters. In this lesson you will learn when a Level Two driver may drive alone, the special exception for work and volunteer emergency service, where a supervisor sits when one is required, and the passenger rules for riders under twenty-one. You will also see that the cell phone ban from Level One rides along unchanged.

lines.text: Five in the morning to nine at night.
Any hour for volunteer emergency service.

narration.text: A Level Two driver may drive alone from five in the morning until nine at night. Outside those hours, driving alone is allowed only when going straight to or from work, or to or from a volunteer fire, rescue or emergency medical service the driver belongs to. Straight means direct. A late shift at a restaurant qualifies, and so does responding with a volunteer fire department, but stopping for a late snack with friends on the way home does not. Outside those cases, the Level Two driver needs a supervising driver for any trip after nine at night.

This trap compares two levels. Level Two is the first level that allows driving alone, and only from five in the morning to nine at night, or when going straight to or from work or a volunteer emergency service. Level One never allows driving alone, even after its first six months. Practice questions sometimes describe a Level One driver with a long-held permit and ask whether a solo daytime trip is fine. It is not. Solo driving begins at Level Two. And at Level Two, solo driving still has hours attached, so a late-night trip for fun needs a supervisor.

lines.text: Every passenger belted or in a child seat.
A required supervisor sits beside you.
Same phone ban as Level One.

narration.text: At Level Two, all passengers must be belted or in a child safety seat. When supervision is required, for example on a late-night trip that is not for work or emergency service, the supervising driver sits beside the driver. And the cell phone rules do not change. Level Two drivers face the same cell phone ban and the same short list of emergency-call exceptions as Level One drivers. So moving up a level gives you hours of solo driving, but it does not give you permission to use a phone behind the wheel. Phones stay down.

lines.text: One more only for a direct school trip.

narration.text: Now the passenger rules. When when driving unsupervised at Level Two, a driver may carry one passenger under twenty-one from outside the household, plus one additional outside passenger under twenty-one who is a student being driven directly to or from school, while there is no under-twenty-one limit when all passengers live in the driver's household. One additional under-twenty-one passenger from outside the household is allowed only when that passenger is a student being driven directly to or from school. So a carpool of two classmates heading straight to school works. A trip to the mall with two friends from other families does not. Passengers twenty-one or older are not counted by this rule at all; the limit is about young riders from other households.

lines.text: Never mix household teens with outside teens.

narration.text: Here is the trickiest part. If every passenger lives in the driver's household, there is no under-twenty-one limit at all, so a teen may drive several younger siblings. But there is a catch. Under-twenty-one household members may not ride along while under-twenty-one passengers from outside the household are aboard. The Level Two limit counts under-twenty-one passengers from outside the household when driving unsupervised. So a teen can carry siblings, or one outside friend, but not a sibling and an outside friend together. Many practice questions turn on exactly this mix.

Here is a quick check: Lee has a Level Two license and is driving alone on a Saturday afternoon. One friend from another family is already in the car, and a second friend from another family also wants a ride to the mall. Can Lee take both? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. Unsupervised, a Level Two driver may carry only one under-twenty-one passenger from outside the household. The second outside rider is allowed only for a student going directly to or from school, and a mall trip does not qualify. One outsider is the limit.

lines.text: Solo from five to nine, or for duty.

narration.text: Let us recap Level Two. It is for drivers at least sixteen but under eighteen, and it is the first level that allows driving alone, from five in the morning to nine at night, or at any hour going straight to or from work or volunteer emergency service. All passengers are belted, and a required supervisor sits beside the driver. Unsupervised, carry one under-twenty-one passenger from outside the household, plus one more only on a direct school trip, while household-only groups have no limit but never mix with outside teens. The phone ban continues.

why_how.text: The Full Provisional License rewards months of clean driving by lifting the hour, supervision and passenger limits.
The phone ban stays until eighteen, because distraction remains a leading risk for young drivers.

scenario.text: Morgan has held Level Two for six months with no moving violation, seat belt or cell phone convictions.

reasoning.text: Morgan meets the six-month hold and the clean-record rule, so Morgan can upgrade online to the Full Provisional License.

result.text: Morgan may now drive at any hour without a supervisor or passenger limits, but still may not use a phone while driving.

claim.text: Many people think the Full Provisional License removes every teen rule, including the phone ban.

correction.text: It lifts the hour, supervision and passenger limits, but a driver under eighteen still may not use a cell phone except for listed emergency calls.

prompt.text: Morgan, seventeen, has the Full Provisional License. Can Morgan answer a friend's call while driving to the store?

answer.text: No. Under eighteen, phone use is still banned except for the listed emergency calls.

rationale.text: The full provisional lifts hours, supervision and passenger limits, not the phone ban for drivers under eighteen.

narration.text: This lesson finishes the graduated licensing path. After Level Two comes Level Three, the Full Provisional License, and eventually a regular Class C license at eighteen. You will learn how long Level Two must be held, the clean-record rule for moving up, how the upgrade is done, which limits the Full Provisional License lifts, and the one important rule that stays in place until eighteen. You will also see what a new North Carolina resident aged fifteen to seventeen should do when arriving with a permit or license from somewhere else.

title.text: Six months and a clean record

lines.text: Hold Level Two at least six months.
No moving, seat belt or phone convictions.

narration.text: A teen must hold the Level Two license for at least six months before applying for the Full Provisional License. As with the earlier step, the record has to be clean. To move up to Level Three, the driver must have had no moving violation, seat belt or cell phone convictions in the previous six months. These are the same three kinds of convictions that blocked the move from Level One. So the habits that matter most in the state's eyes are obeying moving laws, buckling up, and leaving the phone alone, every month, at every level.

lines.text: Level Two hold: at least six months.

narration.text: Here is a numbers trap. A Level Two Limited Provisional License must be held for at least six months before applying for a Full Provisional License. Practice questions love to offer nine months as the Level Two answer, because it is the number learners just memorized. Keep the two holds in order. First you hold Level One for nine months. Then you hold Level Two for at least six months. Nine, then six. The clean-record rule, by contrast, uses the same six-month look-back at both steps, which is a different kind of six.

lines.text: Regular Class C online at eighteen.
Hours, supervision and passenger limits lifted.

narration.text: An eligible driver can upgrade from Level Two to the Level Three Full Provisional License online, and can later upgrade to a regular Class C license online at age eighteen. The Full Provisional License drops the Level One and Level Two limits on driving hours, supervision and passengers. So a full provisional driver may drive late at night, drive alone, and carry friends without the earlier passenger counts. A new North Carolina resident aged fifteen to seventeen who holds a permit or license from elsewhere should contact a local driver license office to learn which permit or license they qualify for.

lines.text: Under eighteen: no phone while driving.

narration.text: One rule survives the upgrade. A Full Provisional licensee who is still under eighteen may not use a cell phone while driving, apart from the same emergency calls allowed at Level One and Level Two. That means a call to an emergency operator, a hospital, doctor's office or clinic, an ambulance service, a fire department, a law enforcement agency, or a parent, legal guardian or spouse. So the Full Provisional License lifts the hour, supervision and passenger limits, yet the phone ban stays until the driver turns eighteen. Freedom grows, but distraction is still off the table.

lines.text: A friend calls during a drive.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Morgan is seventeen and recently upgraded online to the Full Provisional License. While driving alone to the store in the evening, Morgan's phone rings with a friend calling about weekend plans. Can Morgan answer? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. The Full Provisional License lifted the hour, supervision and passenger limits, which is why Morgan can drive alone in the evening, but a driver under eighteen still may not use a cell phone except for the listed emergency calls. A friend's weekend plans are not an emergency.

lines.text: Six months at Level Two, clean record.

narration.text: To finish the graduated path, hold Level Two for at least six months, shorter than the nine-month Level One hold, with no moving violation, seat belt or cell phone convictions in the previous six months. Eligible drivers upgrade online to the Full Provisional License, and online again to a regular Class C at eighteen. The full provisional lifts the hour, supervision and passenger limits, but a driver under eighteen still may not use a cell phone except for listed emergency calls. New teen residents with an out-of-state permit or license should contact a local driver license office.

why_how.text: Provisional licensees are watched more closely because the state wants to catch risky habits early.
For provisional licensees the alcohol rule is any amount at all, with a one-year revocation for a conviction.
School discipline counts too, because the state links responsible behavior at school with the privilege to drive.

scenario.text: Jesse, a seventeen-year-old provisional licensee, drinks one beer at a party and plans to drive home.

reasoning.text: A provisional licensee may not drive after consuming any amount of alcohol, so even one beer bars Jesse from driving.

result.text: Jesse gets a ride instead, avoiding a conviction that would bring a one-year license revocation.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a teen driver is fine as long as they stay under the adult blood alcohol limit.

correction.text: For a provisional licensee the rule is any amount, not a blood alcohol limit, and a conviction means a one-year revocation.

prompt.text: Jesse is a provisional licensee who had one beer an hour ago and feels fine. Can Jesse legally drive home?

answer.text: No. A provisional licensee may not drive after consuming any amount of alcohol.

rationale.text: The provisional rule is any amount, not a blood alcohol limit, so feeling fine does not matter.

lines.text: Zero alcohol, no phone, everyone belted.

narration.text: Some rules apply to every provisional licensee, whatever level they hold. This lesson collects them in one place. You will learn how the DMV watches a young driver's record, the alcohol and drug rule and its penalty, the full phone and texting ban, the seat belt rule for everyone in the car, and the Lose Control, Lose Your License rule that connects school discipline to driving. These rules exist because drivers under eighteen have a much higher crash rate, and each one targets a habit that turns a small mistake into a serious crash.

lines.text: May contact the driver after convictions or crashes.

narration.text: The DMV watches a provisional licensee's driving record more closely than an adult's, and it may contact the driver after certain convictions or crashes. Think of it as an early warning system, a chance to correct problems before they grow. Another rule protects everyone in the car. Everyone riding in a moving vehicle driven by a provisional licensee must have a seat belt properly fastened, in every seat, front and back. If a passenger refuses to buckle up, the trip should not start. The young driver is responsible for the whole car, not only their own seat.

A provisional licensee may not drive after or while consuming any amount of alcohol or drugs. Not a little, not one drink at dinner, not a sip at a party. Any amount. And a conviction brings a one-year license revocation, which can undo all the months of practice and logged hours it took to earn the license. This rule is simpler and stricter than the adult rules covered in the alcohol chapter. A young driver never needs to estimate how much is too much, because for them any amount at all is already too much to drive.

Here is the trap. Many learners know that adults face a blood alcohol limit, and they assume a teen driver can drink a little as long as they stay below it. That is wrong for provisional licensees. For a provisional licensee the alcohol rule is any amount, not a blood alcohol limit, and a conviction means a one-year revocation. On practice questions, watch for options like under the legal limit, half the adult limit, or only beer. All of them are wrong for a provisional driver. The memory line is short and strict: not one drop.

For every provisional licensee, the phone rules are broad. A provisional licensee may not use a cellphone, may not type multiple letters or text to communicate, and may not read email or text messages while driving. Reading counts just as much as writing, so glancing at a new message at a red light is still a violation while driving. The only allowed calls are the listed emergency calls covered earlier. The safest habit is to switch the phone off and put it out of reach before starting the engine, so the temptation never shows up during the drive.

lines.text: School suspension over ten days in a row.

narration.text: North Carolina links school discipline to driving. A student loses their license if suspended from school for more than ten days in a row, or sent to an alternative educational setting for discipline for more than ten days in a row. The loss lasts twelve months. The program is known as Lose Control, Lose Your License, and it is about school discipline, not about traffic violations. A speeding ticket is handled under traffic rules. This rule is triggered by behavior at school, and it reminds young drivers that the license is a privilege tied to responsibility everywhere.

Here is a quick check: Jesse is a seventeen-year-old provisional licensee. At a party, Jesse drank one beer an hour ago, feels completely fine, and believes the amount is well under any adult limit. Can Jesse legally drive home? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. A provisional licensee may not drive after consuming any amount of alcohol, and the rule is any amount, not a blood alcohol limit. How Jesse feels does not matter. A conviction would bring a one-year revocation, so the right move is to get a ride home instead.

Let us recap the rules for every provisional licensee. The DMV watches the record more closely and may reach out after certain convictions or crashes. Everyone in the vehicle must be belted. The driver may not drive after or while consuming any amount of alcohol or drugs, and a conviction means a one-year revocation, because the rule is any amount, not a limit. Phones, texting and reading email or texts are banned while driving. And a school suspension or alternative placement of more than ten days in a row costs the license for twelve months.

why_how.text: A license restriction lets someone drive safely within limits, so going outside those limits is treated like having no license.
Documents prove who you are and where you live, so the DMV checks them carefully and rejects altered ones.

scenario.text: Pat's license is restricted to driving only with special hand controls, but Pat borrows a friend's car without them.

reasoning.text: Going outside the limits of a license restriction is treated as driving without a license.

result.text: Pat should drive only vehicles with the required equipment, or not drive at all.

claim.text: Many people think breaking a license restriction is a minor equipment ticket.

correction.text: A license restriction is a binding limit; breaking it counts as driving without a license, not a minor infraction.

prompt.text: Pat's license requires special hand controls. Pat drives a friend's car that has none. How is Pat treated?

rationale.text: Going outside a license restriction counts as driving without a license, not a minor infraction.

narration.text: This lesson pairs two practical topics. The first is license restrictions, the limits a license can carry so that a person drives safely, and what happens when a driver goes outside them. The second is documents: how the DMV checks them, what a first-time applicant must prove, the insurance proof every applicant shows, and what a card marked Not for Federal Identification means. None of this is about driving skill, but all of it decides whether the license in your wallet is valid for the trip you are making and the places you need to go.

lines.text: Outside the limit counts as unlicensed.

narration.text: A license can be restricted for safety. Common examples are driving only while wearing corrective lenses, or driving only with equipment needed to drive safely, such as special controls. A restriction lets a person keep driving within limits that match what they can do safely. And the limits are real. A driver who goes outside the limits of a license restriction is treated as driving without a license. So the restriction printed on the card is part of the license itself. Drive within it, and the license is valid; drive outside it, and in the law's eyes there is no license.

Here is the trap. Learners tend to think of a restriction as a footnote, so breaking it sounds like a small equipment ticket. It is not. A license restriction is a limit you must stay within, and breaking it is not a minor infraction but counts as driving without a license. This matches what you learned about corrective-lens restrictions in the testing chapter. On practice questions, an option that calls a restriction violation a warning, a minor fault, or acceptable on short trips is the wrong one. The memory line: outside the limit, unlicensed.

lines.text: Name, date of birth and residence.
Social Security number or legal presence.

narration.text: A first-time North Carolina applicant must prove three things: full name and date of birth, a North Carolina residence address, and a Social Security number or legal presence in the United States. Applicants for a driver license must also show proof of vehicle liability insurance. The DMV may copy your documents or hold them briefly to check that they are genuine, and it rejects any document that shows alteration. So bring original, unaltered documents, and expect them to be examined. An altered document is never accepted, no matter how small the change looks.

lines.text: Still valid as a state credential.

narration.text: Some North Carolina cards are marked Not for Federal Identification. A card with that marking is still a valid state license, permit or ID card, so it works for driving in the state. The difference shows up at federal checkpoints. Beginning May seventh, two thousand twenty-five, holders of a Not for Federal Identification card need extra documents to board commercial flights or to enter federal facilities, military bases or nuclear power plants that require identification. So the card answers the question of whether you may drive, but not whether you can board a plane with it alone.

lines.text: Pat borrows a car without them.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Pat's license is restricted to driving only with special hand controls. One weekend Pat's own car is in the shop, so Pat borrows a friend's car, which has no hand controls, for a short trip. How is Pat treated if stopped? Work it out before reading on. The answer is as driving without a license. Going outside the limits of a license restriction is treated as driving without a license, not as a minor infraction, and the short trip does not change that. Pat should use a vehicle with the required equipment.

lines.text: Valid in state, more for federal uses.

narration.text: To wrap up, a license may be restricted for safety, such as corrective lenses or needed equipment, and going outside a restriction is treated as driving without a license. A first-time applicant proves full name and date of birth, a North Carolina residence address, and a Social Security number or legal presence, and shows proof of liability insurance. The DMV may copy or briefly hold documents and rejects altered ones. A Not for Federal Identification card is valid in the state, but since May seventh, two thousand twenty-five, federal uses need extra documents.
